clinicalPearls: A prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma of at least 10 mm, presenting both with hyperprolactinaemia and with mass effects such as headache and visual field loss
Hyperprolactinaemia causes hypogonadism, with oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea in women and reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and infertility in men
Serum prolactin is usually very high and tends to correlate with tumour size, so a large tumour with only modest prolactin elevation suggests a non-functioning adenoma with stalk effect instead
Mass effect on the optic chiasm classically produces a bitemporal hemianopia, and lateral extension can involve the cavernous sinus and cranial nerves
Unlike most pituitary tumours, first-line treatment is medical: dopamine agonists usually shrink the tumour and normalise prolactin, reserving surgery for resistant or complicated cases
A crucial laboratory trap is the hook effect, where extremely high prolactin saturates the immunoassay and produces a falsely low reading unless the sample is diluted
Macroprolactinaemia (aggregated biologically inactive prolactin) is a separate benign cause of raised prolactin and should be excluded to avoid misdiagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: A macroprolactinoma is a benign monoclonal tumour of pituitary lactotroph cells that autonomously secretes prolactin. High circulating prolactin suppresses hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulsatility, lowering LH and FSH and causing hypogonadism and galactorrhoea. As the tumour enlarges beyond the sella it compresses adjacent structures, causing headache, optic chiasm compression with visual field defects, and, by disrupting the pituitary stalk or gland, hypopituitarism. Because prolactin secretion is under dominant inhibitory dopaminergic control, dopamine agonists both suppress hormone output and reduce tumour bulk.
additionalDifferentials: Non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma with stalk-effect hyperprolactinaemia
Physiological or drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia (e.g. antipsychotics, antiemetics)
Other sellar or parasellar masses (craniopharyngioma, meningioma)
additionalInvestigations: Serum prolactin measurement, with serial dilution to exclude the hook effect when a large tumour has apparently modest prolactin
Screening for macroprolactin (e.g. polyethylene glycol precipitation) when clinical picture and level are discordant
Pituitary MRI to define tumour size, suprasellar extension and cavernous sinus invasion
Formal visual field assessment (perimetry) when the tumour abuts the optic chiasm
Anterior pituitary hormone profile to detect coexisting hypopituitarism
Thyroid function and pregnancy testing to exclude secondary causes of hyperprolactinaemia
redFlags: Progressive visual field loss or acute visual deterioration from chiasmal compression
Signs of pituitary apoplexy (sudden severe headache, ophthalmoplegia, collapse)
New or worsening hypopituitarism, including secondary adrenal insufficiency
Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea developing during medical shrinkage of an invasive tumour
reference.prognosis: Most macroprolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normalisation of prolactin, restoration of gonadal function and significant tumour shrinkage; long-term outcome is generally favourable, though some tumours are resistant or require surgery, and lifelong monitoring is usual.
pitfalls: Missing the hook effect and underestimating prolactin in a large tumour, leading to misdiagnosis as a non-functioning adenoma
Operating first when a dopamine agonist would have shrunk the tumour and controlled prolactin
Failing to exclude drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia and macroprolactinaemia before imaging
Overlooking coexisting hypopituitarism, particularly cortisol deficiency, before treatment
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on hyperprolactinaemia
management: First-line medical therapy with a dopamine agonist (cabergoline preferred, or bromocriptine) to normalise prolactin, restore gonadal function and shrink the tumour
Transsphenoidal surgery reserved for dopamine-agonist resistance or intolerance, cerebrospinal fluid leak, or threatening mass effect not responding to medical therapy
Replace deficient anterior pituitary hormones where hypopituitarism coexists, including thyroid hormone, glucocorticoid and sex steroids
Monitoring of serum prolactin, serial pituitary MRI and formal visual field perimetry to track tumour size and chiasmal compression
Management of acute pituitary apoplexy with glucocorticoid cover and urgent surgical decompression if vision deteriorates
Radiotherapy for aggressive or resistant tumours not controlled by medical or surgical means
Pre-conception and pregnancy planning with endocrine input, adjusting the dopamine agonist and monitoring for symptomatic tumour expansion
